chunks: From him, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Ibn Faddal, from Muhammad ibn Ajlan, who said:

A man from the Ansar came to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and said to him: 'I have been tested with a great matter. I had intercourse with my female slave, then I went out for some need of mine. When I returned from the road, I found my boy between the legs of the female slave. She had become pregnant and gave birth to a boy nine months after that.' Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Retain the female slave and do not sell her, and spend on her until she dies or Allah provides for her a way out. If something happens to you, bequeath that she be spent on from your wealth until Allah provides for her a way out. Do not contradict these two reports and the first report, for what it entails is that he should not sell the female slave and keep her. There was no mention of the child in the two reports together, but that confirms the child's attachment to him, because he is not permitted to sell the mother only if the child is his. But if the child is from another man, then it is permissible to sell her in all cases.'

key_terms.أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ ع: Abu Ja'far (AS), referring to Imam Muhammad al-Baqir
key_terms.أُمّ الْوَلَد: Mother of the child (implied context of retaining the slave)
key_terms.لُحُوق الْوَلَد: Attachment/lineage of the child to the father

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling a female slave who has borne a child to her master in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahar clarifies the status of an Umm Walad (mother of a child) in Shia jurisprudence, establishing that the prohibition on selling her is contingent upon the child being the master's offspring. The commentary highlights a nuanced distinction: while the master must retain and support her if the child is his, he retains the right to sell her if the child is from another man, as the bond of lineage (walad) is not established. This ruling underscores the importance of paternity in determining the slave's freedom and the master's financial obligations.
